expectedText:
EMPLOYER'S DUTY TO REIMBURSE BUSINESS EXPENSES — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

ABOUT THIS INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet explains the statutory duty of Acme, Inc. to reimburse Jordan Lee for necessary business expenses under California Labor Code § 2802. It is meant to inform Jordan Lee about the legal framework that applies to work-related expenses. It does not itself request, approve, or certify any specific expense — a separate Business Expense Reimbursement Form is used for that purpose.

THE STATUTORY DUTY TO REIMBURSE
California Labor Code § 2802(a) requires an employer to indemnify its employee for all necessary expenditures or losses the employee incurs in direct consequence of discharging the employee's duties, or of obeying the employer's directions — including a direction later found unlawful, unless the employee believed at the time that it was unlawful. This duty is a general one; the statute itself applies to Jordan Lee's employment with Acme, Inc. to the extent Jordan Lee incurs expenditures or losses of the kind the statute describes.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "An employer shall indemnify his or her employee for all necessary expenditures or losses incurred by the employee in direct consequence of the discharge of his or her duties, or of his or her obedience to the directions of the employer, even though unlawful, unless the employee, at the time of obeying the directions, believed them to be unlawful."
  — California Labor Code, Cal. Lab. Code § 2802(a) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2802.)
  Known gap: This clause states the general statutory duty; it does not determine whether any particular expense reported by the employee qualifies as a 'necessary expenditure or loss' — that depends on the facts of each expenditure. The interest clause and the definition/fee-shifting clause elsewhere in this document quote different subsections ((b) and (c)) of this same Labor Code § 2802; they are not independent statutory sources from this clause, only different parts of the same section, and are disclosed here as such rather than presented as separate corroboration.

INTEREST ON UNPAID REIMBURSEMENT
Under Labor Code § 2802(b), any award made by a court, or by the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement, to reimburse necessary expenditures under this section carries interest at the same rate as a civil judgment. That interest accrues from the date the employee incurred the expenditure or loss, not from the date of any later award or demand.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "All awards made by a court or by the Division of Labor Standards Enforcement for reimbursement of necessary expenditures under this section shall carry interest at the same rate as judgments in civil actions. Interest shall accrue from the date on which the employee incurred the necessary expenditure or loss."
  — California Labor Code, Cal. Lab. Code § 2802(b) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2802.)
  Known gap: This clause describes only how interest is calculated once an award is made under the statute; it does not state whether the employee is owed reimbursement for any particular expense, and it does not address the procedure for obtaining such an award. It quotes subsection (b) of the same Labor Code § 2802 discussed in the statutory-duty clause elsewhere in this document — the two clauses are not independent sources, only different subsections of one statute.

DEFINITION OF "NECESSARY EXPENDITURES OR LOSSES" AND ATTORNEY'S FEES
Labor Code § 2802(c) defines the term "necessary expenditures or losses," as used throughout the statute, to include all reasonable costs — expressly including, but not limited to, attorney's fees — that an employee incurs in enforcing the reimbursement right created by this section. A fee award for an employee who enforces the statute is therefore written into the statute's own text, not left solely to a court's general discretion.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "For purposes of this section, the term “necessary expenditures or losses” shall include all reasonable costs, including, but not limited to, attorney’s fees incurred by the employee enforcing the rights granted by this section."
  — California Labor Code, Cal. Lab. Code § 2802(c) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2802.)
  Known gap: This clause quotes only subsection (c)'s definition and fee-inclusion language; it does not address the legal standard a court applies to determine whether an employee has succeeded in enforcing the statute, or how a reasonable fee amount is calculated in a given case. It quotes the same Labor Code § 2802 discussed in the statutory-duty and interest clauses elsewhere in this document — these are different subsections of one statute, not independent sources.

THE RIGHT CANNOT BE WAIVED BY PRIVATE AGREEMENT
Labor Code § 2804 — a separately numbered section within the same article of the Labor Code as § 2802 — provides that any contract or agreement, express or implied, by which an employee purports to waive the benefits of that article (which includes § 2802) is null and void. The same section states that the article does not deprive an employee of any right or remedy otherwise available under California law.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "Any contract or agreement, express or implied, made by any employee to waive the benefits of this article or any part thereof, is null and void, and this article shall not deprive any employee or his personal representative of any right or remedy to which he is entitled under the laws of this State."
  — California Labor Code, Cal. Lab. Code § 2804 (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displaySection.xhtml?lawCode=LAB&sectionNum=2804.)
  Known gap: Section 2804 is an independently numbered Labor Code section, not merely a different subsection of § 2802, so it is presented here as a genuinely separate statutory source rather than a restatement of it. This clause states only that a private, prospective waiver of the article's benefits is void; it does not address distinct legal doctrines — such as the settlement or release of an already-existing, disputed claim — that can operate differently from a prospective waiver and are outside the scope of this document.

APPLICATION TO PERSONAL CELL PHONES AND REMOTE WORK
In Cochran v. Schwan's Home Service, Inc. (2014) 228 Cal.App.4th 1137, a California Court of Appeal held that when an employer requires employees to use their personal cell phones for work-related calls, § 2802 requires the employer to reimburse a reasonable percentage of the employee's cell phone bill. The court held that this obligation applies whether the employee's cell phone plan has unlimited minutes or limited minutes, and that it does not matter whether the phone bill is paid by the employee personally or by someone else. The court left the calculation of the specific reasonable percentage owed in any given case to the trial court and the parties.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-04]
  "requires the employer to reimburse them. Whether the employees have cell phone plans with unlimited minutes or limited minutes, the reimbursement owed is a reasonable percentage of their cell phone bills."
  — Cochran v. Schwan's Home Service, Inc., 228 Cal. App. 4th 1137 (2014) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2717454/cochran-v-schwans-home-service-inc/)
  "It does not matter whether the phone bill is paid for by a third person, or at all."
  — Cochran v. Schwan's Home Service, Inc., 228 Cal. App. 4th 1137 (2014) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/2717454/cochran-v-schwans-home-service-inc/)
  Known gap: Cochran addressed personal cell phone expenses in the context of a class-certification appeal; the Court of Appeal expressly left the calculation of any specific percentage or dollar figure to the trial court and the parties in each case, and this document does not state what percentage of any specific employee's phone bill is owed. Cochran's reasoning was stated in terms of personal cell phone use specifically; this document has not independently verified that the same reasoning has been extended by a published California decision to other remote-work expenses such as home internet, home office equipment, or utilities, and readers should not assume that extension has been confirmed here. Cochran is a Court of Appeal decision; the California Supreme Court denied the losing party's petition for review (S221319, denied November 25, 2014) without issuing its own published opinion on the question. This is a genuinely independent source from Labor Code §§ 2802 and 2804 cited elsewhere in this document — it is case law construing the statute, not another subsection or cross-referenced provision of the statutory text itself.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT OF RECEIPT
Jordan Lee acknowledges having received this information sheet describing reimbursement rights and obligations under California Labor Code § 2802.

Employee: Jordan Lee
Signature: _______________________________________________
Date: _______________

On behalf of Acme, Inc.:
Signature: _______________________________________________
Date: _______________
